\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{पलाण्डुः} (palāṇḍuḥ)}{पलाण्डुः (palāṇḍuḥ)}]{\sk{पलाण्डुः} (palāṇḍuḥ) — an onion}

\label{lesson:SA-C108-palanduh}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for ginger, then the Sanskrit for garlic.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{पलाण्डुः}}
\textbf{\sk{पलाण्डुः}} — \emph{palāṇḍuḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}an onion\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{palāṇḍu} \textquotedblleft{}an onion\textquotedblright{} appears from the law book of Manu on (MW). MW gives no derivation beyond the grammarians, so its origin is uncertain. Pali kept it as \emph{palaṇḍuka} (CDIAL 7954).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for this chapter.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Sanskrit for ginger, then the Sanskrit for garlic, then say \emph{palāṇḍuḥ} again

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{आलुकम्} (ālukam)}{आलुकम् (ālukam)}]{\sk{आलुकम्} (ālukam) — a potato}

\label{lesson:SA-C108-alukam}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for garlic, then the Sanskrit for an onion.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{आलुकम्}}
\textbf{\sk{आलुकम्}} — \emph{ālukam} — \textquotedblleft{}a potato\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{āluka} is \emph{ālu} with the suffix \emph{-ka}, an old word-list name for an edible root, the elephant-foot yam (CDIAL 1388). The potato reached India from the Americas only in modern times, and the languages moved the old name onto it: Hindi \emph{ālū} \textquotedblleft{}potato\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 1388). MW gives no source for \emph{ālu}, so its origin is uncertain.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for this chapter.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ālukam}, once more

\end{itemize}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{वृन्ताकम्} (vṛntākam)}{वृन्ताकम् (vṛntākam)}]{\sk{वृन्ताकम्} (vṛntākam) — an aubergine}

\label{lesson:SA-C108-vrntakam}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for an onion, then the Sanskrit for a potato.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{वृन्ताकम्}}
\textbf{\sk{वृन्ताकम्}} — \emph{vṛntākam} — \textquotedblleft{}an aubergine\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{vṛntāka} \textquotedblleft{}the aubergine\textquotedblright{} is one of several Sanskrit names for the plant gathered in CDIAL 9369. CDIAL 11503 thinks the names probably share one origin and, after LM, gives it as Dravidian, while DEDR 5301 lists \emph{vṛntāka} beside Dravidian words for the brinjal. Its sister form \emph{vātiṅgaṇa} travelled west as Persian \emph{bādingān} and lives on as Hindi \emph{baigan} (CDIAL 11503).
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{कूष्माण्डम्} (kūṣmāṇḍam)}{कूष्माण्डम् (kūṣmāṇḍam)}]{\sk{कूष्माण्डम्} (kūṣmāṇḍam) — a pumpkin}

\label{lesson:SA-C108-kusmandam}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for a potato, then the Sanskrit for an aubergine.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{कूष्माण्डम्}}
\textbf{\sk{कूष्माण्डम्}} — \emph{kūṣmāṇḍam} — \textquotedblleft{}a pumpkin\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{kūṣmāṇḍa}, also \emph{kuṣmāṇḍa} (MW), is a pumpkin-gourd. CDIAL 3374 explains it as a Sanskritized form of a Prakrit word of non-Aryan origin. That Prakrit word lives on as Hindi \emph{kohṛā} and Bengali \emph{kumṛā} \textquotedblleft{}pumpkin\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 3374).
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{नारिकेलम्} (nārikelam)}{नारिकेलम् (nārikelam)}]{\sk{नारिकेलम्} (nārikelam) — a coconut}

\label{lesson:SA-C108-narikelam}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for an aubergine, then the Sanskrit for a pumpkin.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{नारिकेलम्}}
\textbf{\sk{नारिकेलम्}} — \emph{nārikelam} — \textquotedblleft{}a coconut\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{nārikela} \textquotedblleft{}coconut\textquotedblright{} is borrowed from Dravidian: CDIAL 7075, after Bloch, takes it from a Dravidian compound, comparing Tamil \emph{nāri} \textquotedblleft{}fibre\textquotedblright{}. It lives on as Hindi \emph{nāriyal} and Marathi \emph{nāreḷ} \textquotedblleft{}coconut\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 7075).
\end{cousinweb}
